vignette:
Daniel Mercer, a 49-year-old architect, came to treatment after months of feeling increasingly on guard in the very places where he was supposed to feel competent and calm. The event he described happened two years earlier, while he was walking through a downtown transit concourse on the way back from a client meeting. A fight broke out near a kiosk, and in the confusion a man was thrown hard against the tile floor and kept hitting his head while other people shouted and stepped back. Daniel had not been the target, but he had stood close enough to see the impact, smell the sharp mix of sweat and something metallic in the air, and feel a wave of nausea rise in his own stomach. Since then, violence of any kind, even a raised voice in a crowded lobby, could make him tense in the instant; the smell of spilled alcohol or stale urine in a station restroom, or the sickly odor that reminded him of that afternoon, pulled him back into the scene with an intensity that made his body react before he could think. He said that when he remembered the event, it did not stay in the past: the images came disordered and incomplete, and he could not put the memories in the right order or find words that felt adequate to explain what had happened.

As those fragments returned, Daniel became more vigilant, as if his mind were trying to protect him by staying a step ahead of danger. He scanned for exits whenever he entered a restaurant, conference room, or office tower, and he preferred to sit with his back against a wall where he could see the whole room. That way, he believed he would not be caught off guard again. He described feeling jumpy in meetings, startled by a chair scraping the floor or a dropped tool on a construction site, and said the moment he felt his body brace, the event would flash back with a force that made it seem as if it were happening right now. The confusion in his memory fed that alarm: because he could not sequence what he saw, he felt he had no reliable account of it, and the uncertainty made the scene feel even more unfinished and immediate. At the same time, his own threat monitoring narrowed what he noticed. Once he was looking for danger, he was more likely to catch the smell, the sudden movement, the edge in another person’s voice, and each of those cues sharpened his sense that something violent might erupt again.

Over time, Daniel came to interpret his reaction as evidence that the event had exposed something fundamental about him. He had come to believe there was something about him that made bad things happen, that he had somehow been in the wrong place, looked away at the wrong moment, or failed to act quickly enough. He also felt increasingly isolated and set apart from other people, especially when colleagues spoke casually about crowded trains, late-night bars, or incidents they had witnessed without being shaken. Those beliefs made the world feel less predictable and made him watch even more closely for danger. He found himself avoiding certain routes downtown, standing near doorways in client presentations, and noticing particular smells before anything else. In the office, he would pause at the entrance to a conference room, scan the exits, and choose a seat where his back was protected. The more he did this, the more ordinary spaces seemed dangerous, and the more quickly a whiff of the wrong cleaning product or a burst of yelling could send his attention straight back to the concourse scene. The memories then arrived with their old force: broken sequence, no words, the sense that he was right back there.

By the time he sought help, Daniel said his life had become smaller and more effortful. He still performed well enough at work, but he avoided after-hours site visits and felt ashamed that he was increasingly dependent on controlling where he sat and where he stood. He had not told many people why, because he could not easily explain what he felt and because speaking about it seemed to summon the event into the room. What brought him in was the fear that he could not stop bad things from happening to him and the worsening sense that the world would keep cornering him unless he stayed permanently alert. He wanted relief from the constant scanning, from the nausea that could rise in a crowded space, and from the feeling that his own mind was trapping him back in that afternoon.
